before_record.label: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and fall of the monarchy
before_record.meaning: The sectional central committee became an insurrectionary Commune, sent fédérés and the democratized National Guard against the Tuileries, defeated the Swiss Guards, and forced suspension of the monarchy. The tocsin revived the recognized insurrectionary signal of 1789. Guards died in combat, retreat and supposed safe custody, while some survivors later became September prison victims. The monarchy was provisionally suspended pending a Convention and the royal family confined in the Temple; formal abolition came later.
before_record.stance: The source presents 10 August as the bloodiest and most decisive revolutionary journée to that point, transferring power away from king and Assembly alike.
acceptable_access: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and fall of the monarchy

evidence.evidence_summary: The Brunswick threats, distribution of arms, deposition petitions, and Brissotin retreat prepare the insurrection.

The tocsin signaled insurrection, the Commune’s forces took the Tuileries, and Swiss Guards died in fighting, retreat and supposed custody. The Assembly suspended the monarchy pending a Convention; the royal family entered close custody in the Temple.
Effective power after the uprising lies with the Paris Commune rather than the Assembly.
Surviving defenders later form one politically identified group among massacre victims.

before_record.label: Paris, the provinces, and national sovereignty
before_record.meaning: The Convention's dependence on Parisian popular power made the constitutional relation between the capital, elected national representatives, and the departments the chapter's central conflict. Sections and the democratized National Guard supplied coercive power, but Paris was internally divided: Muscadins briefly captured several sectional assemblies. Departmental-guard proposals sought protection for national deliberation; the same sectional forms served opposing provincial coalitions. Sectional pressure joined claims of popular guardianship to immediate subsistence demands, compelling the Convention to adopt grain and bread controls.
before_record.stance: Paris created and protected the Republic but could also coerce its representatives; provincial resistance claimed to defend national representation and local autonomy rather than simply to reject republican unity. An urban section was not inherently Montagnard, and indivisible-republic rhetoric was shared by competing camps.

before_record.label: Legislative Assembly, political trajectory and loss of authority
before_record.meaning: The Assembly began with locally experienced but nationally little-known deputies, drove confrontation over priests, émigrés, and war, and then lost practical authority to popular and communal power before the Convention met. Its deputies were often nationally obscure but had acquired revolutionary administrative experience; composition belongs within this institutional trajectory. The deputies were predominantly property-owning lawyers and younger than their predecessors.
before_record.stance: The source rejects the departing deputies' condescension toward the new body, but shows that its authority collapsed during the crises it helped create.
acceptable_access: Legislative Assembly, political trajectory and loss of authority

evidence.evidence_summary: Introduces the Assembly's social composition, local revolutionary experience, and priorities.
Provides the Assembly's occupational, social, generational, and experiential profile.
Clerical resistance and emigration are identified as the deputies' most urgent opening problems.
Deposition and Lafayette questions move beyond the deputies' ability to manage them.
The Assembly watches the 10 August insurrection helplessly and suspends the monarchy after the palace falls.
With most deputies absent, the remaining Assembly yields to the new Paris Commune during its final weeks.

evidence.evidence_summary: Irish invasion fears helped trigger a bank run, while Saint Vincent eased panic. Spithead/Nore sailors sought pay and conditions, with no firm evidence of subversion; many of the same vessels and crews then destroyed the Dutch fleet at Camperdown, restoring confidence in naval defense. The run reflected anxiety over loans to unsuccessful allies and was triggered by an emergency Irish-defense loan; gold payments remained suspended after the panic eased.

Crisis and war-weariness renewed British peace proposals. Pitt would recognize French European conquests and restore gains taken from France overseas, but would not also surrender all Dutch and Spanish colonial acquisitions without compensation.
Uses Camperdown to qualify British desperation and show that Britain could continue the war alone.

before_record.meaning: Bonaparte's pragmatic recognition of religion's political power, his conciliatory treatment of Catholic practice, and his use of Church reconciliation to stabilize France. Pius VI’s captive death encouraged a mistaken Parisian expectation that the papacy would disappear; the Venetian conclave and election of Pius VII demonstrated institutional resilience and opened a more promising path to reconciliation.

proposed_record.label: Bonaparte's religious policy and the road to reconciliation with Rome
proposed_record.meaning: Bonaparte recognized religion’s political power and used reconciliation with the Church to stabilize France. Popular Catholic observance revived after 1795 despite official anticlericalism; revolutionary religious reorganization had left a deep, persistent domestic wound. Pius VI’s death in captivity prompted mistaken Parisian predictions of papal extinction, while the Venetian conclave and election of the pragmatic Pius VII opened a path to negotiation. Bonaparte’s instrumental approach included displaying adherence to Islam in Egypt and advising gradual treatment of religion like property. Quiet relaxation of compulsory décadi observance in favor of Sunday prepared reconciliation, publicly celebrated at the Easter 1802 mass in Notre-Dame. Negotiations faced foot-dragging from ministers including Talleyrand, an apostate former bishop, and Fouché, a priest turned dechristianizer.

evidence.evidence_summary: Religious practice had revived since 1795 despite renewed official anticlericalism, while division over the Church remained the Revolution’s deepest persistent wound. When captive Pius VI died, many in Paris assumed he would have no successor and the institutional Church was collapsing. Bonaparte instead recognized religion’s political power and the Church’s resilience.

The Venice conclave elected the pragmatic Pius VII, refuting predictions of papal extinction. Bonaparte’s earlier restraint, quiet relaxation of compulsory décadi observance, funeral honors for Pius VI and public Catholic assurances prepared negotiations. Without personal faith, he displayed adherence to Islam in Egypt to support French rule and advised gradual treatment of religion like property.

Reconciliation is intended to separate religion from counter-revolution and conciliate populations incorporated into France. Negotiations also faced foot-dragging from Talleyrand and Fouché, respectively an apostate former bishop and a priest turned dechristianizer.

before_record.label: Revolutionary Armies, coercion and dissolution
before_record.meaning: Paris and provincial Revolutionary Armies enforced requisitioning, suspect policy, economic controls, repression, and dechristianization before centralization reduced and dissolved them.
before_record.stance: These were politically recruited local coercive forces, not ordinary field armies; the Paris force's provincial deployment was exceptional.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention activated Revolutionary Armies under popular pressure to confront hoarders and rural resistance.
Ronsin, closely aligned with Hébert, received command of the Paris force.
Provincial forces reached roughly 40, 000 and served as local instruments of intimidation, arrest, and repression.
Centralizing legislation abolished unofficial local forces and retained only a single closely supervised army.
The Law of 14 Frimaire reduced the armies to a centrally supervised force and began winding up local units.
The Paris Revolutionary Army was dissolved after the Hébertist defeat, relieving groups it had terrorized.
